_about: Each entry puts one known bug back into the CLI and the suite must fail. The set covers the two things the CLI is responsible for: refusing an action whose consequence is that a child stops being locked out, and telling the truth about the machine. A mutant here that survives is not a coverage gap -- it is a safety refusal that no test would notice being removed.

mutants.note: TakeFirst stops hoisting the positional at all, so `plock unlock casey --minutes 5` parses as five positionals and zero flags -- the documented form silently stops working

mutants.old: if i+1 < len(args) && flagWantsValue(fs, a, name) {
mutants.note: the rule is inverted, so a boolean flag swallows the token after it and a value-taking flag leaves its value to be taken as the account name -- the override is granted to the wrong account
the flag is dropped instead of kept, so fs.Parse never sees it and never reports the typo -- an unknown flag becomes silently ignored

Go's %-*s never truncates, so the rendered width is max(pad,len(label)) either way: with the guard pad=max(width,len), giving max(max(width,len),len)==max(width,len); without it pad=width, giving max(width,len). Identical for every input, so no test can distinguish them. The guard is defensive against a formatter that did truncate, not load-bearing against fmt. Verified by running both variants and diffing the output. the label column stops widening to fit, so values are printed over each other and a report that looks parsed is not
an override can be granted to an account that is not managed. It is not harmless: it sits in the file, and if that username is created next week it is already active with a stale reason attached
`plock lock --all` on its own is refused, so the documented lock-everyone form can never be typed
a profile can be removed while children are assigned to it, leaving them with no schedule and therefore no lockout -- the silent release
a user can be assigned to a profile that does not exist, which means they are enabled for enforcement and enforced by nothing
a brand new managed user starts unenforced, so the first `user assign` on a fresh install does nothing at all
the writer's own refusal is discarded, so the command prints `removed` over a document it did not change

mutants.new: if err := cfg.ValidateForEdit(); err != nil && false {
mutants.note: the write gate is removed entirely, so a command can write a document the daemon then refuses to load

mutants.old: fmt.Fprintf(stderr, "plock profile: unknown subcommand %q\n\n%s", sub, profileUsage)
mutants.note: the unknown-verb message loses the word that says what went wrong, so a typo reads as a result
the "it is not working" check disappears: a machine where every child is unlocked during a lockout reports a clean bill of health
--json can be combined with --try, so a monitoring job reading JSON can lock a child's screen on a schedule
doctor exits 0 whatever it finds, so it is useless in a script and misleading in a bug report

mutants.old: rep.add(okCheck("config.loads", fmt.Sprintf("%s parses as version %d", *path, cfg.Version)))
mutants.new: rep.add(skipCheck("config.loads", fmt.Sprintf("%s parses as version %d", *path, cfg.Version)))
mutants.note: a document that loaded successfully is reported as unchecked, so a reader cannot tell a read config from one the tool never managed to open
an enabled account whose profile does not resolve is never reported, so a child locked out by nothing looks configured
an account disabled on purpose is reported as a failure, which trains the operator to ignore the check
a locked screen is reported as unenforced and an unlocked one is not -- the check inverted, which is worse than absent
a session this build cannot lock stops being reported during an open window
a world-readable config holding the admin credential and every schedule is accepted
a non-regular file at the config path is accepted, though the daemon refuses it
the directory is not checked, so the read-only-parent case -- where config.Save cannot rename over the document -- is missed
a poll interval of hours stops being warned about, so a window opening goes unnoticed for that long
an expired certificate is reported as valid, and the browser refuses the page without saying why

mutants.new:
case "active":
		return warnCheck("daemon", "the plock service is active", "")
mutants.note: a running daemon stops being reported as ok, so the one line the operator scans for is buried among warnings

default:
		return okCheck("daemon", fmt.Sprintf("the plock service is %s", state))
mutants.note: an inactive or failed service is reported as fine -- the single most common reason the screen never locks
a failure is filed under warned, so --json's `failed` array is empty on a broken machine and the exit code stays 0
the dangling account is not named, so the operator cannot tell which child is unmanaged
the report stops being sorted, so two runs of doctor on the same machine produce output that cannot be diffed

A machine with no systemd is reported as running an unknown service rather than as not checked, sending the operator to look for a service that was never there. TestSystemdStateSeparatesNoSystemdFromCannotAsk/systemctl_missing
the state word is discarded when systemctl exits non-zero to report it, so `inactive` becomes an error rather than an answer
the certificate is never decoded, so every custom-TLS check reports an unreadable file

mutants.old: Seat: s.Seat, Locked: s.Locked, Lockable: platform.IsLockable(s),
mutants.new: Seat: s.Seat, Locked: s.Locked, Lockable: true,
mutants.note: status claims every session is lockable, so a remote or seatless session reads as one the daemon could lock

mutants.new:
rest = append(rest, a)
			if false && len(after) > 0 {
mutants.note: the separator stops protecting the positional. This is the reported bug verbatim: every one of the 17 call sites reads found=false plus leftover args as the operator mistyping, so `unlock --minutes 5 -- casey` is refused while the doc comment promises it

the `--` itself dropped from the args handed to flag.Parse. The positional is still adopted, so the obvious case passes -- but the remainder is re-parsed as flags, and `unlock -- casey --minutes 5` silently honours a flag the separator said was a word
the separator overwrites a positional already taken, so `unlock casey -- anna` operates on anna. The first name typed is the one the operator meant

the unclaimed-argument guard disabled. This is the data-loss path: `plock user rm -- bob --config /tmp/test.json` drops --config on the floor and edits /etc/plock/config.json while the operator believes they named a scratch file

the round-2 blocker: the writability check is written, unit-tested and documented at docs/cli.md:282, and never registered -- so a green `plock doctor` reads as "the daemon can save this" on a read-only mount or a full filesystem. Killed by TestDoctorRunsTheWritabilityCheck and its --json twin, both of which assert the check RUNS rather than that the check is correct.
backends marshals as null again -- declared, documented at docs/cli.md:80, never assigned. null is worse than absent: it reads as "this machine offers nothing" rather than "this command did not ask".
a typo in settings.lockBackends reaches the text report through Warnings but vanishes from the JSON field a monitoring job reads

mutants.old: r.Field("backends", "none — settings.lockBackends is empty, so nothing can be locked")
mutants.note: an empty backend list renders as a bare `backends` label, which is the exact shape the never-assigned field produced. Killed only by an assertion scoped to the backends LINE: a whole-output Contains(out, "none") is satisfied by the unrelated "none — the config has no users" line, and that version of the test passed against this mutant.

stop folding a concatenated *Usage const. unlockUsage is built with `+`, so it disappears from the text map and every flag beside it -- including --minutes -- goes unchecked while the test reports itself as covering the package. This is the blindness the reviewer found, pinned so a future refactor cannot reintroduce it as a tidy-up.

mutants.old: if lit, ok := call.Args[0].(*ast.BasicLit); ok && lit.Kind == token.STRING {
mutants.note: restore the flag-kind allowlist. fs.Int("minutes") sits outside it again, so --minutes leaves the checked set and its help text becomes unenforced. The rule is structural now -- any FlagSet method whose first argument is a string literal declares a flag -- precisely so a new kind cannot be silently unlisted.

forget the package's own FlagSet helper. manage.go declares its flags on `c.fs`, a selector rather than the plain `fs` identifier, so all eight profile/user flags become invisible to the documentation test.

stop reading newFlagSet's usage argument. The flags are still collected and then thrown away, because declaredFlags drops any function whose const it cannot resolve -- so the documentation test checks less and still passes. Killed by the attribution guard, which asks whether every declared flag reached a const. The body keeps `rhs` read: an unused variable is a build failure, and the runner reports that as a non-zero exit like any other catch.

narrow the synopsis back to line prefixes. profileUsage wraps a long invocation and its continuation line carries [--all-day] [--disable], which a `plock ` prefix test cannot see -- that version reported two documented flags as missing. Kept used so the mutant is a narrowing, not a compile error.

the deployment-shape check is written but never added to the report: `plock doctor` prints a clean bill of health on a machine where a daemon started from this terminal will decline the account in front of the operator, and docs/cli.md still promises the line. TestDoctorRunsTheDaemonSliceCheck, TestDoctorJSONCarriesTheDaemonSliceCheck.

an active system service stops counting as 'outside every login session', so doctor warns about a declined account on the one deployment the shipped unit is designed for -- the machine where the rule is inert. A check that cries wolf here is a check the operator learns to scroll past. TestCheckDaemonSlice/service_active_operator_in_a_login_session.

the slice flag is ignored, so every machine with no service running gets warned about an account it will not decline -- including a root shell in system.slice, where no account can ever be declined. TestCheckDaemonSlice/no_service_operator_outside_any_session.

the warning stops naming the uid it is declining, which turns an actionable sentence into a generality: the operator runs doctor precisely to find out WHICH account is going unenforced. TestCheckDaemonSliceNamesTheAccountNotTheShell.

`plock lock --all` never warns, so the operator learns the self-session rule by losing the desktop they were typing on -- which is the sentence the warning exists to replace. TestLockAllWarnsWhenItIsAboutToLockYourOwnSession.

mutants.new:
if true {
		if self := lockSelfLocation(); self.InUserSlice {
mutants.note: the warning escapes the --all scope and fires when the operator names their own account, where it is not news; a warning that fires on the deliberate case stops meaning anything on the sweep. TestLockOneUserDoesNotWarnAboutTheNameTheyTyped.

mutants.old: fmt.Fprintf(stderr, "plock lock: --all includes your own session (%s), so your "+
mutants.new: fmt.Fprintf(stdout, "plock lock: --all includes your own session (%s), so your "+
mutants.note: the warning moves onto stdout and lands in front of the --json document, so every script that reads `plock lock --all --json` fails to parse it -- the same reason the missing-backend warning is on stderr. TestLockAllWarningDoesNotPolluteJSON.
MainPID matched anywhere in the line: systemd prints ExecMainPID as well, and it comes first, so the decoy is stopped at and answered 0 -- 'no daemon' on a running service. TestParseMainPID

An inactive unit reported as 'no init system here' rather than 'systemd answered and nothing is running' -- the collapse the two flags exist to prevent, and the one that hides 'the service is stopped' behind a hedge. TestAskDaemonLocation
A failed cgroup read reported as a known location: the report then renders 'running in a system slice, no session is declined', the reassurance with nothing behind it. TestAskDaemonLocation

mutants.old: refused := daemonState{SystemdKnown: true, AskFailed: true, Err: err}
mutants.note: A systemctl that was found and refused reported as no init system reachable -- the problem the tool was asked to look for, invented. TestAskDaemonLocation/systemctl_refusing_to_answer_is_neither_running_nor_stopped and TestStatusSaysSystemdRefusedRatherThanNotRunning

The self-session rule dropped from the session rows: a lockable session the engine deliberately declines renders as an ordinary unlocked session, which is the blank the issue was opened for. TestStatusMarksTheSessionTheDaemonRunsIn, TestStatusTextPutsTheDeclineReasonOnTheRowItExplains
The known-ness half dropped, so a mark rests on a location the report itself calls unverified. TestStatusMarksNothingWhenTheDaemonLocationIsUnverified

The unreadable-slice warning silenced: the sessions below are then unmarked with nothing saying why, and an unmarked list reads as 'declines nobody'. TestStatusSaysItCannotTellRatherThanDecliningNobody

The engine-inside-a-login-session wording dropped, so the report falls through to 'no session is declined' for a daemon that is declining one right now. TestStatusTextPutsTheDeclineReasonOnTheRowItExplains
'no init system reachable' collapsed into 'not running': the report tells an operator with an unreachable bus that their service is stopped. TestStatusSeparatesNoSystemdFromNotRunning
The slice-unknown wording dropped, so an unreadable location falls through to the system-slice sentence and asserts that nothing is declined. TestStatusSaysItCannotTellRatherThanDecliningNobody

An unreadable cgroup falling through to the system-slice sentence: doctor tells an operator that no account is declined on evidence that it could not read anything, which is the reassurance this check exists to withhold. TestCheckDaemonSlice/service_active,_cgroup_unreadable

A unit running inside somebody's login session reported as the shipped system unit, so the account that will never be locked is certified as enforced. TestCheckDaemonSlice/service_active_inside_a_login_session

if state == "active" || state == "activating" {
		switch d := daemon(); {
mutants.new:
if false && (state == "active" || state == "activating") {
		switch d := daemon(); {
mutants.note: The active branch skipped, so a running service is reasoned about as a shell: the check answers the manual-start question about a machine where the daemon is already up, and its answer is the operator's own slice rather than the daemon's. TestCheckDaemonSlice/service_active,_operator_in_a_login_session

mutants.old: refused := daemonState{SystemdKnown: true, AskFailed: true, Err: err}
mutants.note: A refusal recorded as 'systemd answered', which renders as "not running" and marks no session declined -- the assertion the state was added to prevent. TestAskDaemonLocation/systemctl_refusing_to_answer_is_neither_running_nor_stopped

Classification back on error prose instead of the sentinel. ExecRunner rewrites exec's wording, so the prose match misses the real 'no systemctl' error and a box with no init system is reported as one whose service is stopped. TestAskDaemonLocation/no_systemd_is_not_the_same_answer_as_not_running

The kernel's answer thrown away because the call around it failed: a refusal that printed a pid anyway still has a location, and dropping it makes the report less true than the machine. TestAskDaemonLocation/a_refusal_that_printed_a_pid_still_has_a_location

doctor's other half of the same prose match: on a machine with no systemctl it warns 'could not ask systemd' and sends the operator to look for a broken bus instead of the absent init system. TestSystemdStateSeparatesNoSystemdFromCannotAsk/systemctl_missing
The refused ask falling through to the sentence it does not license. TestStatusSaysSystemdRefusedRatherThanNotRunning
A location read from /proc printed with no mention that systemd refused, so the report reads as though the init system confirmed it. TestStatusKeepsARefusalsLocationAndSaysWhereItCameFrom

`plock profile add --copy-from X` carries X's display name onto the copy and exits 0, which is the one way to build from a shell the exact pair the web rename form refuses. `plock profile edit --name` sets a name with no collision check, so renaming an existing profile onto a name another profile already answers to succeeds from the CLI while the same rename is a 422 on the page. TestProfileEditRefusesANameAnotherProfileHas.
